# Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta (SN 42)

**ID:** SN 42  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul7.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul7.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Gāmaṇisaṁyutta* (SN 42) is the forty-second chapter of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Saḷāyatanavagga* [Bodhi 2003; Jerryson et al. 2017]. The collection comprises thirteen discourses centered on conversations between the Buddha and various village headmen or chieftains (*gāmaṇi*) [Bodhi 2003]. Many of the interlocutors represent specialized occupations—such as the mercenary commander Yodhājīva, horse trainers, and the actor-manager Tālapuṭa—or seek out the Buddha with adversarial intent, attempting to debate him or questioning whether monastics should accept gold and silver [Bodhi 2003; Jerryson et al. 2017]. Key topics discussed include the karmic destiny of warriors and performers, the futility of brahmanical funeral rituals, the cultivation of loving-kindness, and craving as the root of suffering (as illustrated through the sorrow that arises from attachment to loved ones in SN 42.11) [Flores 2008; Jerryson et al. 2017]. In each case, the Buddha gently dispels their preconceptions through measured reasoning and ethical analysis [Bodhi 2003].

Twelve discourses in the collection possess parallels across Chinese and northern Buddhist collections, primarily within the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and the "Alternative" *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 100), with two discourses (SN 42.6 and SN 42.13) paralleled in the *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26, MĀ 17 and MĀ 20).

In modern scholarship, the *Gāmaṇisaṁyutta* is widely cited in discussions of early Buddhist perspectives on warfare and state violence [Bartholomeusz 2002; Jerryson et al. 2017]. In particular, the Buddha's rejection in SN 42.3 of the belief that fallen soldiers attain heaven—pointing out that killing in battle stems from debased, hostile intentions leading to lower rebirth—has served as a foundational proof text for scholars analyzing early Buddhist anti-war ethics [Bartholomeusz 2002; Jerryson et al. 2017]. Additionally, the trumpeter simile (*saṅkhadhama*) in SN 42.8 illustrates the boundless nature of the immeasurable mental liberations (*appamāṇa*), a formulation examined in discussions of Buddhist meditation practice and later scholastic treatises [IABU 2012].

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha: A New Translation of the Samyutta Nikāya (2003) — Structural position in the Samyutta, characterization of the inquirers as headmen, commentary notes on names like Caṇḍa and Tālapuṭa.
- [Flores 2008] Ralph Flores, Buddhist Scriptures as Literature: Sacred Rhetoric and the Uses of Theory (2008) — Analysis of craving as the root of suffering in SN 42.11 using the example of Cirvāsi's mother.
- [IABU 2012] Buddhist Philosophy and Meditation Practice: 2nd IABU Conference (2012) — Discussion of the trumpeter simile and mettā cetovimutti in SN 42.8 and its parallels.
- [Bartholomeusz 2002] Tessa J. Bartholomeusz, In Defence of Dharma: Just-war ideology in Buddhist Sri Lanka (2002) — Scholarly debate regarding Schmithausen's use of the Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta as a proof text against warfare.
- [Jerryson et al. 2017] Michael K. Jerryson, Mark Juergensmeyer, and Margo Kitts, Violence and the World's Religious Traditions: An Introduction (2017) — Discussion of SN 42.3 (Yodhājīva) regarding warrior ethics and karmic intention.
- [Bodhi 2012] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha: A Complete Translation of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (2012) — Comparison of the grouping of grounds for praise and blame between SN 42.12 and AN parallels.
